title: New Zealand Inflation Eases in Q3
body: New Zealand's annual inflation rate eased to 3.7% in the third quarter of 2026, down from 4.1% in the previous quarter and slightly below market expectations of 3.8%. Despite this moderation, inflation remains above the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 1–3% target range. Petrol was the single largest contributor to annual inflation, surging 19.1% amid higher international oil and fuel prices linked to conflict in the Middle East. The cost of building new homes rose 3.2%, reflecting increased material, subcontractor, labour, and fuel costs. Electricity prices climbed 9.3%, international airfares were up 12.5%, and local authority rates and payments increased 6.2%. These rates, which are measured annually in the September quarter, have been a significant driver of inflation in recent years. On a quarterly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.7%, a marked slowdown from the 1.5% increase recorded in the second quarter. title: Argentina's EMAE Contracts for Second Straight Month
body: Argentina's economic activity contracted by 1.7% year-on-year in August 2026, deepening from a 1.4% decline in July and defying expectations for a 0.3% increase. Of the 15 sectors surveyed, 10 registered declines, with fishing recording the sharpest drop at 15.7%. Manufacturing output fell 3.2%, while wholesale and retail trade and repair activities decreased 3.5%. Financial intermediation shrank 3.8%, transport and communications were down 2.9%, and tax-related revenues declined 4.2%. By contrast, five sectors posted annual growth. Mining and quarrying led the gains, expanding 11.1%, followed by electricity, gas and water, which rose 4.3%, and hotels and restaurants, up 3.1%. On a month-on-month basis, the EMAE (Monthly Estimator of Economic Activity) edged up 0.1% in seasonally adjusted terms, partially recovering from a 2.9% drop in July. title: Ibovespa Falls as Election Uncertainty Weighs

The survey also indicated that 52% of respondents would "never" vote for Bolsonaro, versus 47% for Lula, whose rejection rate dropped six percentage points in a week. Despite the lack of detailed policy proposals from Bolsonaro, investors see his candidacy as more likely to deliver fiscal reforms that could support lower interest rates. body: Brent crude climbed back above $109 a barrel on Wednesday, erasing earlier losses in a turbulent session as attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure intensified across the Middle East. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said naval mines had forced three tankers to halt after they attempted to use routes Tehran considers unauthorized, while the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a vessel had been struck near Oman. Despite mounting security risks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said shipments through the Strait of Hormuz were nearing prewar levels, and data from Kpler and Vortexa indicated that overall Middle Eastern exports have risen since the summer. US EIA data showed crude inventories declined by just over 3 million barrels last week, undershooting the 4.9 million-barrel draw reported in industry figures. title: Oil Wavers Below $98 as Supply Recovers
body: Crude oil prices slipped back below $98 a barrel on Wednesday after briefly touching $100 in a highly volatile trading session. The market is coming under pressure from rising crude exports out of the Middle East, where producers have stepped up shuttle shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Tanker-tracking data show that seaborne flows from the region have now exceeded pre-war levels. Saudi Arabia's crude exports climbed 7.9% in August, reaching their highest level since March. At the same time, Russia is preparing to send its first diesel cargo to the United States on Thursday under an agreement between Presidents Trump and Putin. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is also exploring cooperation with India's Reliance Industries to refine Western energy supplies. Nonetheless, geopolitical tensions across the Middle East remain elevated, and record-high freight rates in the Persian Gulf continue to lend support to crude prices, limiting the extent of the recent pullback. title: BoE preview: MUFG expects November rate hike as energy shock pushes UK inflation above 4%
body: A hike on November 5 would extend the energy-driven tightening seen across central banks. Any guidance pointing to a February follow-up would likely support sterling, particularly against currencies where central banks are seen as slower to respond. Gilts look the more vulnerable asset: 10-year UK yields already sit at the top of the G7 range, and further tightening alongside reduced fiscal headroom ahead of the Budget could keep pressure on longer-dated debt. For equities, higher rates and energy costs weigh on domestically focused UK stocks, while the FTSE 100's energy-heavy constituents offer some offset. Oil and gas remain the key swing factor: with household energy bills driving the expected rise in inflation, any further spike in prices linked to the Middle East war would strengthen the case for a longer hiking cycle. --- Earlier: UK September CPI inflation rises to 3.5%, reinforces BOE November rate hike expectations --- MUFG says the Bank of England cannot look through this energy shock the way it might like, because the UK economy is simply too strong to make waiting look safe.

Any hint that the cycle is nearing its end could weigh on the currency. For equities, a pause offers some relief to rate-sensitive sectors. The semiconductor-led export boom underpinning growth keeps chipmakers at the centre of the market's growth story. title: BlackRock's Hambro sees gold rising on debt and deficits
body: Hambro's view adds a heavyweight institutional voice to the fiscal-debasement case for gold. It suggests that dips driven by shifting rate expectations may be treated as buying opportunities rather than a change in trend. His argument that mining costs are rising more slowly than the gold price supports the case for further margin expansion and equity outperformance across the sector, including copper producers. The buyback criticism carries weight given BlackRock's large stakes in Newmont, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields. It could push gold majors toward more flexible capital returns, or toward redirecting cash into new mine development. For bond markets, his warning that governments will need to pay higher interest to attract lenders points to continued upward pressure on longer-dated yields. - BlackRock's Evy Hambro sees gold as insurance against governments that cannot stop borrowing, and he wants the gold miners to spend their windfall more wisely than those governments do.
